summary: Offers observations on simple best-effort traffic, loosely defined as Internet traffic not covered by quality-of-service mechanisms, congestion-based pricing, cost-based fairness, or admission control. It argues that best-effort traffic plays a useful role in the Internet and is worth keeping, and discusses how it relates to differentiated treatment.

plainLanguage.summary: Best-effort is like a public road open to all, with no reserved lanes. This paper says that is a good thing worth keeping, even if some drivers also get special lanes.

subtitle: Why the Internet's simple, classless approach to traffic is worth keeping

tldr.problem: Simple best-effort traffic—Internet traffic with no special quality-of-service treatment—has limitations like inability to guarantee delivery or quality. But quality-of-service mechanisms are complex to deploy and raise economic and technical challenges.
tldr.mechanism: This document argues that simple best-effort traffic paired with rough flow-rate fairness (achieved naturally by TCP's congestion control) is a useful service model worth preserving alongside higher-quality options, not replacing it.
tldr.outcome: Best-effort should remain a foundational traffic class in the Internet, supported by mechanisms to achieve basic fairness, while other service classes can be added as supplements rather than replacements.

today: RFC 5290 is an Informational document published in July 2008. Best-effort traffic remains the dominant service class on the Internet. Quality-of-service mechanisms have been deployed in some networks, but as supplements to best-effort rather than replacements for it, reflecting the principles this document advocates.

sections.title: What is Simple Best-Effort Traffic
sections.content:
Simple best-effort traffic is Internet traffic that does not rely on quality-of-service mechanisms, congestion-based pricing, cost-based fairness, or admission control. It uses end-to-end transport protocols like TCP and UDP with minimal network requirements.

This is different from specialized traffic classes like IntServ or DiffServ, which use differential scheduling in routers to give some traffic higher priority or better performance. The document argues that the simple best-effort model has been the dominant traffic class in the Internet for over 20 years and remains valuable despite its limitations.
sections.plainLanguage: Best-effort traffic is the normal kind of Internet traffic that just does its best without any special handling—like sending a postcard instead of requiring a signed delivery.

sections.title: Why Simple Best-Effort Traffic Works
sections.content:
Simple best-effort traffic makes minimal demands on network infrastructure. Routers do not need special scheduling, queue management, or enforcement mechanisms—they can use simple first-in-first-out queuing. It also makes minimal economic demands, relying on basic peering relationships among Internet Service Providers.

Importantly, simple best-effort traffic has proven useful in practice for over 20 years, supporting everything from file transfer and email to web traffic, video streaming, and voice communications. While not optimal, it has allowed users to share network resources fairly and prevented collapse of the network during congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: Simple best-effort works because routers do not need to be complicated, ISPs can easily cooperate, and the system has proven it can handle all kinds of Internet traffic.

sections.title: Flow-Rate Fairness and Congestion Control
sections.content:
In the current Internet, rough flow-rate fairness—the idea that different data flows should get roughly equal bandwidth—is achieved because most traffic uses TCP, and most TCP implementations use conformant congestion control algorithms.

The document explains that this rough fairness emerges naturally from TCP's behavior rather than being enforced by the network. TCP connections slow down when they detect congestion (through packet loss), which prevents any single flow from consuming all available bandwidth. This means different applications and users get a reasonable share without the network having to make intelligent scheduling decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP is like cars on a road that slow down when it gets crowded, so everyone gets a turn to use the highway fairly.

sections.title: Challenges and Open Questions
sections.content:
The document identifies several limitations of flow-rate fairness. First, it is hard to enforce in existing networks designed for simple best-effort service. Second, there is no consensus on what exactly should be fair—the granularity of a flow, how to account for different round-trip times, how to handle flows crossing multiple congested routers, or whether to measure fairness in packets per second or bytes per second.

Another major challenge is deployment. Adding quality-of-service mechanisms requires coordinating changes across many independent networks and organizations, involving complex economic relationships and infrastructure upgrades. This makes incremental deployment extremely difficult.
sections.plainLanguage: It is hard to decide exactly what fairness should mean and even harder to change the whole Internet to enforce it.

sections.title: Related Standards and Research
sections.content:
The document reviews IETF standards and research literature relevant to best-effort traffic. IETF documents like RFC 896 on congestion control, RFC 2914 on congestion control principles, and RFC 3714 on fairness all discuss these issues. The document also references academic research on fair queueing, congestion-based pricing, and TCP fairness.

Throughout, the theme is that the Internet community has long recognized both the value and the challenges of simple best-effort service.
sections.plainLanguage: Many researchers and standards groups have studied this problem over the years.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content:
The authors conclude that simple best-effort traffic deserves to be preserved as a core Internet service, even as organizations add higher-quality service classes for specific needs. The combination of best-effort service with rough flow-rate fairness through TCP has proven effective and should not be replaced.

The document emphasizes that quality-of-service mechanisms can be useful as supplements—providing premium service for applications that need it—without eliminating the simple, fair baseline that serves all users equally.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep the simple fair system for everyone, even if you add fancy fast lanes for special traffic.
